court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: A widow who had run a boarding house both before and continuously after her marriage was held entitled to recover from her deceased husband's estate for board and lodging she furnished him, based on his written acknowledgment of the debt. The court treated her boarding-house business as her separate, ongoing enterprise and enforced the husband's recognized obligation to pay for the support she furnished.

quotes.text: She purchased the house and continued to take boarders, and always had either boarders or lodgers from that time until the present. She received the money from her boarders, purchased her own supplies and ran the house in the same manner that she had conducted the same prior to her marriage.

Held, that the wife was entitled to recover from her husband’s estate the amount specified in the acknowledgment of indebtedness, no objection having been made that such amount did not represent the value of the board and lodging so furnished;

notes: Occupancy duration of the boarders generally is not stated (only that the husband was boarded 17 years); marked unclear since the case centers on long-term family support, not short-term letting, but affirms boarding-house keeping as a lawful ordinary business with enforceable compensation.
